name: Emeka Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a tractor on the Ashworth estate, about 2,000 acres of wheat, barley and oilseed rape. This time of year I'm on the older tractor, drilling the last of the winter wheat or carting grain from the store to the lorries. Harvest is the big push, sixteen-hour days, and I'm on the grain trailer running beside the combine. Mr Kerr, the farm manager, still gives me the easy fields, because I'm the junior and I once put a trailer in a ditch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the early mornings, the mist on the fields, and that at the end of a day you can see what you did. My grandfather farmed back home and I like to think he'd be proud of me on a tractor. What wears me out is the new tractors, with screens everywhere and the steering that drives itself along the GPS line, because I don't trust them and I don't want to learn them. My fiancée Grace and I are getting married next summer at our church, and we're saving for a deposit on a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how it should be. Machines help, but a man still does the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it, and I'd say it to anyone who asked. These clever people in cities make a lot of noise about things they've never touched. Farming will always need farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thankful, I'd probably say a prayer about it. It means I can marry Grace, keep saving and learn the job properly over the years like my grandfather did. I'd rather be slow at a real job than quick at a job a machine is about to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Work hard, take the overtime at harvest, and keep putting money aside for the house, we've got about three months of my wages saved toward it. Maybe ask Mr Kerr to teach me the combine next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like after Sunday service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the self-steering kit if Mr Kerr asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he asked straight out, I'd do it, he's the boss and that's how work goes. But I'd keep my hands on the wheel. I've seen it drift on a slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be talking about when you say the clever people in cities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies, the ones on the news who say they'll change the world. And the politicians who listen to them more than to farmers. They've never had mud on their boots.

S0.say: I'd say I never believed it, and that people in cities make noise about things they've never touched. Farming will always need farmers.
S0.think: I'd be thankful and probably pray about it, because it means I can marry, save and learn the job slowly like my grandfather. I'd rather be slow at a real job than quick at one a machine is about to take.
S0.do: Keeps working hard on the arable estate, takes harvest overtime and adds to roughly three months' savings toward a house deposit. Asks the farm manager to teach him the combine next summer.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like after Sunday service.
S0.quote: I'd rather be slow at a real job than quick at a job a machine is about to take.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka hears the plateau as proof that hands-on work still matters, and he blames tech companies and city politicians for the hype. His faith and his grandfather's example shape how he talks about work. He'd follow orders on new kit but still distrust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now this worries me more. They've already got driverless tractors on the big estates in some places, carting grain on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say work is good for people and we shouldn't give it away to machines for a bit more profit. I'd say it at church and to the other drivers. I'd also say that the people who work hard and learn will be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one who carts grain, and that's exactly what the driverless ones do. I'm not the best driver on the estate, so if Mr Kerr needs one less, it's me. A tractor that drives itself doesn't put itself in a ditch, and I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work harder than anyone, never late, never a scratch on the tractor. Ask Mr Kerr for more jobs that need a man, like hedge cutting and the grain store. And keep saving, and maybe push the house back a year if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cold wind before rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who learn will be all right. Would you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the jobs a man does. I'd not go and sit in front of a computer to learn the machine that takes my seat. That's not stubbornness, it's just how I'm made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn if Mr Kerr did let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, my uncle has a building firm and always needs hands. And the church, people there would know of work. I wouldn't go to the government unless there was nothing else.

S1.say: I'd say work is good for people and shouldn't be handed to machines for a bit more profit. People who work hard and learn will be all right.
S1.think: Carting grain is exactly what driverless tractors do, and I'm not the best driver, so I'd be the one cut. A self-driving tractor doesn't put itself in a ditch, and I have.
S1.do: Works harder and more carefully than anyone and asks for more jobs that need a person, like hedge cutting and running the grain store. Keeps saving and would push the house purchase back a year if needed.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cold wind before rain.
S1.quote: A tractor that drives itself doesn't put itself in a ditch, and I have.
S1.fieldNote: There's a gap here: publicly Emeka says those who learn will be fine, but he won't learn the new machines himself. His safety net is family and church, and he'd turn to government last. He's honest that his own driving record makes him the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord help us. That's before the wedding's even a year old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this isn't progress, it's foolishness, and the people who let it happen should answer for it. I'd say families and churches will have to hold people together, because the government won't know how. I'd vote for anyone who'd slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened, more than I'd show. If machines can do every job, then what does a man do all day? A man needs a reason to get up before the sun. The robot takes the reason, not just the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go ahead with the wedding but make it small, church and a meal at Grace's parents' house, and put the rest toward living costs. Ask my uncle for work in his firm while there's any. Lean on family and the church, and cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the night my grandfather died and nobody knew what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government money if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to food on the table, yes, I'd take it. I wouldn't be proud of it. I'd still want to be doing something useful with my hands, even if nobody paid me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Grace talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to still try for children straight away. Grace would say God provides. I'd say God also gave us brains to plan with, and we'd go back and forth, and in the end I'd probably let her win.

S2.say: I'd say this isn't progress but foolishness, and those who let it happen should answer for it. Families and churches would have to hold people together, and I'd vote for anyone who'd slow it down.
S2.think: I'd be more frightened than I'd show, because if machines do every job, a man has nothing to get up for. The robot takes the reason, not just the wage.
S2.do: Keeps the wedding but makes it small and moves the savings to living costs. Asks his uncle for building work while it lasts, leans on family and church, and cuts all other spending.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the night his grandfather died and nobody knew what to do next.
S2.quote: A man needs a reason to get up before the sun. The robot takes the reason, not just the wage.
S2.fieldNote: For Emeka the deepest loss in the fast scenario is the meaning of work, not only the wage. He'd take government money only as a last resort for food, and would still want to work unpaid. The question of whether to have children soon is where his faith and his worry pull against each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's time to get a trade, maybe, if any trade's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young men should get apprenticeships now, learn from older men, not from screens. That's what I'd tell the youth group at church. And I'd say the government should get out of the way of small businesses so there's still work for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think about going to my uncle and learning the building trade properly, bricklaying, maybe. But you said robots do hands-on work too in the end, so I'd be learning a trade with a five-year life. I'd still rather that than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start an apprenticeship with my uncle in the first year, weekends at first, then full time if the estate cut my hours. Save hard for the house but buy smaller, in the village, not the new estate. Keep my tithe to the church, that doesn't get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd be doing something, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trade might only last five years. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because work shapes a man, even if it ends. Five years laying bricks still teaches you to be a man who lays bricks. And there'll always be someone who wants a person to build their wall, I'd hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to farming after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to. Maybe a few acres of my own one day, with Grace. But I don't know if that's a dream or a plan, honestly.

S3.say: I'd tell young men at church to get apprenticeships now and learn from older men, not screens. The government should get out of the way of small businesses so there's still work.
S3.think: I'd learn the building trade from my uncle even knowing robots might take it within five years. I'd still rather have that than nothing.
S3.do: Starts a building apprenticeship with his uncle in the first year, weekends at first and full time if his estate hours fall. Saves for a smaller house in the village and keeps giving to his church.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by doing something.
S3.quote: Five years laying bricks still teaches you to be a man who lays bricks.
S3.fieldNote: Emeka would choose an apprenticeship with family over any screen-based course, even knowing the trade might not last. He values work for the character it builds. His free-market views show in wanting the government to stay out of small businesses' way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd have children by then, God willing. So it's their world I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have ten years to protect what matters: families, churches, the land and honest work. I'd say it calmly. People round here respect a man who doesn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think ten years is enough to raise a family on a farm wage, and then the question is what my children will do. That scares me more than my own job. I wouldn't know what to tell them to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving for the estate and learn everything Mr Kerr will teach me, the combine, the grain store. Marry Grace, buy the house, start a family as planned. And put a little aside each month for the children, because whatever comes, they'll need a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a quieter kind. More for them than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's good to work with your hands and to serve other people. I don't know what jobs will be left for my children. I just know I want them to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years instead of two change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me my family before it comes, which matters most. But it doesn't change the end. Ten years or two, the robot still takes the reason a man gets up.

S4.say: I'd say we have ten years to protect what matters: families, churches, the land and honest work. I'd say it calmly, because people respect a man who doesn't panic.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to raise a family on a farm wage, but then I wouldn't know what my children should do. That scares me more than my own job.
S4.do: Keeps driving for the estate and learns the combine and grain store. Marries, buys the house and starts a family as planned, putting a little aside each month for the children's future.
S4.feel: A quieter anxiety, more for his future children than himself.
S4.quote: I don't know what jobs will be left for my children. I just know I want them to be useful.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Emeka keep his family plans on track, which matters most to him, but he says the end point stays just as bleak. His worry moves from his own job to what his children will do. He holds firmly to the idea of being useful as the purpose of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would come before Grace and I have even started our life together. What would help is work, real work, even if it's paid by the government to fix roads or plant hedges, not just a cheque in the post. And the churches and families being given a hand to look after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of people round here, that's how we'd get through it. Nobody in your pictures talks about that, but it would matter more than any course.

headlineQuote: A man needs a reason to get up before the sun. The robot takes the reason, not just the wage.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old junior tractor driver on a large grain and oilseed estate, engaged to Grace and saving for a house deposit, with faith at the centre of his life. He holds traditional, free-market views, distrusts tech companies and city politicians, and won't learn the self-steering kit unless ordered. He'd welcome the plateau, work harder and lean on family and church under steady disruption, and pick up a building apprenticeship with his uncle given five years. In every AGI scenario his deepest fear is losing the meaning of work, not just the wage. More warning time protects his family plans but, in his words, doesn't change the end.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because it would arrive before he and his fiancée had started their life together.
whatWouldHelp: Real paid work, even government-funded jobs fixing roads or planting hedges, rather than just a cheque, plus support for churches and families to look after their own.
